title: Juice Spacecraft Uses Earth's Gravity to Head Toward Jupiter
summary:
A spacecraft named Juice got a boost from Earth on September 28. Juice is short for Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer, a mission run by the European Space Agency, or ESA. It used Earth's gravity to bend its path toward Jupiter and gain speed. This is called a gravity assist, and it helps save fuel.

The flyby changed Juice's direction by 20 degrees and increased its speed by 3.5 kilometers per second. During the four weeks before the encounter, controllers needed only one small course correction. They had set aside six chances to adjust its path.

At its closest point, Juice passed 8,640 kilometers above the Indian Ocean. Its monitoring cameras took a series of pictures.

Angela Dietz, Juice's Spacecraft Operations Manager, explained that careful planning meant the team used only a small amount of the fuel reserved for this flyby. That leaves more fuel for studying Jupiter's icy moons later.

Changing direction was the main goal, but the flyby also let the team test Juice's science instruments. Earlier testing opportunities came during a lunar-Earth gravity assist in 2024 and observations of Comet 3I/ATLAS in 2025.

Teams spent months planning when each of Juice's 10 instruments could work. Project scientist Claire Vallat explained that the team had to choose which activities came first. For example, Juice relied only on battery power while in Earth's shadow. Tests that helped prepare the instruments for Jupiter received priority.

At Jupiter, Juice is scheduled to make 35 flybys of the large moons Ganymede, Callisto and Europa. Earth served as a rehearsal to help scientists prepare for those encounters.

Juice also spent several days traveling through Earth's magnetotail. This is the long part of Earth's magnetic field that stretches away from the Sun.
why_it_matters: The Earth flyby saved fuel and helped scientists test instruments before Juice studies Jupiter's icy moons.
